claims.text: The patient presented on 07/01/26 with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset following physical exertion, characterized as throbbing and diffuse with associated mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, engages in regular jogging, denies smoking or recreational drug use, and consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines in immediate family, though the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.

Initial triage and examination on 07/01/26 recorded a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examination on 07/01/26 was unremarkable, showing the patient alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficits, normal cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 07/01/26 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 07/01/26 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 07/01/26, the patient was admitted to the Neurology ward with a working diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) and a plan to start oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours.
On 07/01/26, the patient reported persistent headache rated 7/10 with blood pressure of 150/92 mmHg; blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 07/01/26, the management plan included continuing nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours and adding potassium chloride 1 g orally twice daily to correct hypokalemia.
The patient's GP was contacted at 20:00 on 07/01/26 to provide an update on admission and the preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.

On 08/01/26, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS; the patient reported headache severity reduced to 5/10, with blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, CRP 12 mg/L, and persistent mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L).
On 08/01/26, the nimodipine dose was adjusted to 30 mg every 4 hours, potassium chloride 1 g twice daily was continued, and a repeat MRA was planned for 48 hours later.
On 08/01/26, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.
On 09/01/26, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 3/10 with blood pressure 125/80 mmHg; blood tests from 08/01/26 showed mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L).
On 09/01/26, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating MRA in 24 hours.
On 09/01/26, the rehab team assessed the patient and noted mild residual neck stiffness with no significant functional impairments, deciding to arrange outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.

On 10/01/26, the patient reported headache severity reduced to 2/10 with blood pressure 125/80 mmHg; the plan was to maintain nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, continue dietary measures for hyponatremia, and repeat MRA on 11/01/26.
On 10/01/26, the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs, and demonstrated understanding of the information.

On 11/01/26, the patient reported headache severity of 2/10 with blood pressure 125/78 mmHg; the plan was to continue nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours and perform a repeat MRA to confirm resolution of vasoconstriction.
A repeat MRA performed at 10:30 on 11/01/26 showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS and leading to a decision to plan discharge for 12/01/26.
On 12/01/26, the patient reported no further headaches with blood pressure 130/80 mmHg; the repeat MRA from 11/01/26 confirmed resolution of vasoconstriction.

On 12/01/26, discharge was planned with a regimen of nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks, and advice to avoid known triggers.
On 12/01/26, the GP was contacted to discuss discharge, during which a discharge medication of amlodipine 5 mg once daily and a follow-up appointment in 4 weeks were discussed.

Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 documents a plan for nimodipine 30 mg four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, while note-18 documents a discussion with the GP regarding amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
